query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Hybrid ML-informed thermodynamic integration can compute liquid and solid free energies with full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–phonon effects at strongly reduced cost compared to both direct ab initio MD and TOR-TILD for multi-component (≥4 elements) high-entropy alloys near melting points, while maintaining free-energy accuracy within a few meV/atom of pure ab initio benchmarks.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys (e.g., Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni) in a representative single-phase or near single-phase condition.
generation.intervention: Train a machine-learning interatomic potential on limited, targeted ab initio molecular-dynamics data, then couple that ML potential with accelerated thermodynamic integration to predict solid and liquid free energies and derived properties (e.g., melting temperature, heat capacities).
generation.conditions: Temperatures spanning from ~0.5 to 1.1 × Tmelt of each high-entropy alloy composition, ensuring inclusion of both stable solid phase(s) and the fluid state in the sampling.
generation.structural_mediator: Use short ab initio MD simulations to seed the ML potential’s training set, capturing relevant short-range order and fluctuating local structures, especially near solid–liquid transitions.
generation.mechanism: With the ML potential capturing interatomic forces accurately for relevant configurations, low-cost thermodynamic integration over the sampled phase space can incorporate vibrational entropy, anharmonic contributions, and electron–phonon couplings. This mimics ab initio sampling at a fraction of the computational expense.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD, the method will cut computational time by an order of magnitude for high-entropy alloys while preserving free-energy differences to within a few meV/atom, thus yielding comparable melting and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
generation.baseline: Current ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD workflow results for elemental or binary systems with established free-energy benchmarks validated against experiments.
generation.boundary: Applicable to multi-principal-element alloys of up to five components over temperature ranges from room temperature up to and slightly above their melting point. May require additional refinement for systems with strong chemical short-range ordering or more than five principal elements.
generation.uncertainty: Sampling efficiency gains may vary depending on the complexity of local order and the available ab initio reference data distribution. Uncertainties up to a few meV/atom in free energy (and ~10–50 K in predicted melting temperature) may occur if training data do not sufficiently cover relevant configurations.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare single- and multi-component high-entropy alloy free energies from the proposed ML-based thermodynamic integration with direct ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD over a range of temperatures. Perform a blind test on a carefully selected HPC resource to measure computational expense and accuracy relative to existing methods.
measurements: Free energies (solid, liquid, and near transition)
Melting points derived from predicted free-energy differences
Computational wall time and resource usage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based approach requires similar or greater computational time than TOR-TILD or yields more than ~5 meV/atom deviation in free energies or >5% error in predicted melting temperature relative to ab initio references, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.
